source.title: Data-Constrained Language Model Pretraining: Improved Regularization and Scaling Laws
source.authors: Zhiwei Xu; Shi-Hao Wu; Hanseul Cho; Wei Hu; Yi-Xin Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling fits in a data-constrained, repeated-data regime and reports that the additive Chinchilla form is misspecified there; it proposes and evaluates a coupled alternative.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own validation-loss scaling measurements and fits, held-out scaling-law predictions, and downstream evaluations. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows. Table 8 code-data losses are not extracted because they report MIR-versus-baseline outcomes rather than a scaling-law fit; the paper's stated result is that MIR lowers loss at all five sizes.
record.test_reason: The study fits candidate scaling laws to its own 5-size × 4-budget repeated-data grid and an external grid. It argues and shows that the additive Chinchilla form is misspecified when unique data is fixed and repeated, and that a coupled power-law form fits better. This bears on V5 (repeated data), V7 (form and fitting dependence) and, over a short data-axis holdout, V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it omits two findings. The authors also report that large weight decay brings dLLMs and AR models to comparable loss. They estimate MIR's gain at about 1.3× unique data at the 200M–400M budgets under SoftQ, with downstream gains at 1.4B.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than reproduce the original abundant-data, compute-optimal scaling experiments, the study examines fixed unique-data budgets with repeated epochs and per-cell regularization tuning, and fits a new coupled law.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected scaling law and MIR data-efficiency estimates depend on the functional form and fitting protocol. Data-efficiency estimates differ across Chinchilla, Quanta, Muennighoff-style, and SoftQ fits; the main Muennighoff comparison uses a dataset-adapted two-stage protocol rather than the original fixed-C4 coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1.4B and 100M unique tokens, the MIR model beats the strongly regularized baseline on 6 of 8 zero-shot metrics (BoolQ +10.2 points), with the others mixed or within error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Masked-input regularization can improve some downstream scores at a fixed size and data budget; this is not a test of downstream predictability.

fits_no_version.finding: MIR lowers validation loss relative to the strongly regularized AR baseline at all sizes from 72M to 1.4B, and on Stack-V2 code data. Strong weight decay closes the AR–dLLM gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-constrained training, regularization recipe choices shift the loss curve. This is a method comparison, not a scaling-law test.

record.problems: The experiments span only up to 1.4B parameters and 400M unique tokens; the authors note this is small relative to frontier-scale pretraining. They hold architecture and optimizer fixed and rely on heavy per-cell hyperparameter search. The held-out data-budget extrapolation is from 100M/200M/300M to 400M, not several orders of magnitude. The study does not report uncertainty intervals for its scaling-law fit metrics.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: Table 8 Stack-V2 baseline/MIR losses by size, because those results report MIR effects on code-heavy data without fitting or evaluating a scaling law. Table 4 AR/dLLM recipe comparisons concern regularization and model-objective comparison rather than the claim's scaling-law versions. Individual held-out residuals in Appendix B.3 Table 12 were not separately recorded; the aggregate held-out fit metrics are included in r20–r23.

untested.parts: All runs are in a data-constrained, repeated-data regime with fixed unique data, so the condition that the other resources are not the bottleneck is never met. There is no compute axis. Model sizes span about 1.3 orders of magnitude (72M–1.4B).
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude. The only holdout is 300M→400M unique tokens.
Not tested: no fixed-compute allocation analysis.
Not tested: architecture shape is fixed along the scaling ladder.
Image and video models, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Only repeated-data language-model pretraining is.
Not tested. Downstream results are one MIR vs baseline comparison at 1.4B.
Parameter-counting choices and compute-optimal split dependence are not tested. The WSD vs cosine schedule choice is not analysed for its effect on fitted laws.

missing.what: Loss-gap diagnostic: L(N,U)−L(N,400M) grows with model size, whereas Chinchilla predicts a constant gap. This is the core misspecification evidence.
Fitted exponents shift across splits and grids. Chinchilla β is 0.29 on the full grid vs 0.19 on the held-out split; Chinchilla α is 0.52 on DCLM vs 1.16 on the Kim et al. grid.
The literal fixed-C4 Muennighoff coefficients fit much worse than the dataset-adapted protocol: RMSE 0.060 on the DCLM full fit, 0.072 held-out, 0.120 on the Kim et al. grid.
Data-efficiency ratios at 100M–300M under each law. Chinchilla gives 0.70× at 100M, against 0.92–1.15× for the other laws.
Power-law-with-offset fits over five model sizes at 100M: R² 0.9993 for the baseline and 0.9987 for MIR.

record.verdict_notes: Every run is in a data-constrained, repeated-data regime, so the evidence belongs to V5 (repeated data) and V7 rather than V1. The reader's V1 links and labels are removed. The reader's 'challenges' label for Chinchilla under V7 is reversed: Chinchilla's misfit is evidence that form choice matters, so it supports V7. Chinchilla's degraded but non-failing fit supports limits_scope rather than challenges for V2 and V5. Rows r24–r27 are in-sample fits, not extrapolations. Rows r11–r14 are fits on the study's own MIR runs and report no fit quality. Scale is small: at most 1.4B parameters and 400M unique tokens.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines validation-loss scaling with model size and unique-data size in a data-constrained setting. It does not test loss scaling with training compute, or the abundant-data setting where the other resources are not bottlenecks.
The holdout is the 400M-token data budget, predicted from 100M/200M/300M points at the same five model sizes; it does not test extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget optimization of parameter and token allocation is reported.
Architecture details are held fixed across experiments rather than varied at fixed parameter count.
The study tests a data-constrained, repeated-data language-model regime. It does not test image or video models, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream results compare MIR with a regularized baseline at one model size; the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The study compares candidate scaling-law forms and fitting protocols in this data-constrained setting. It does not test parameter-counting choices or a fixed-compute optimal split.
